why: `build.target` in ruvyxa.config.ts sets the JavaScript language level, and
two compilers apply it: crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/compiler.rs for the
client graph and packages/ruvyxa/runtime/compiler.mjs for the server and
prerender graph. A project renders through whichever one built it, so the
two must not disagree about which values are configurable — a value one
accepts and the other refuses is a build that succeeds on the client and
fails at prerender, or worse, two halves of one page compiled to different
language levels.
The key spent several releases accepted and inert: it was validated and
carried into BundleOptions, and consumed by neither transform. The Rust
side built TransformOptions::default() and compiler.mjs hardcoded
target: 'esnext', so a project that set es2018 got byte-identical esnext
output and found out in the browser.
es5 is absent from the accepted list because oxc does not implement it;
`every_accepted_es_target_is_one_oxc_accepts` checks the list against the
transformer rather than against this comment.
What a target *costs* is not in this table, because it is a property of
the source rather than of the number: ordinary application code compiles
helper-free at es2022 and above, a private class field pulls
@oxc-project/runtime helpers in from es2021 down, and one `using`
declaration needs one at every target below es2026. Both hosts refuse the
emitted code when a helper import appears, since Ruvyxa ships no helper
runtime and a deployed function bundle resolves no bare specifiers.
An unset value is not in `rejected`: it means the default, and each host
spells absence in its own way (None on one side, an unset environment
variable on the other). An empty string is a host that set the value
wrong and is refused by both.
